ch23.title: The Confession of Thomas
ch23.b001: A Week on the Slopes of Olivet
ch23.b002: Thomas Didymus was walking the hills again. On the eastern slopes of Olivet the April grass stood knee-high, and the almond blossoms had already fallen. He did not count his steps. A man who had always counted and measured everything counted nothing at all that week. When the sun rose he walked; when he was worn out he went back to the home of Simon in Bethpage and slept; when he woke he walked again. Apart from the people of that house and John Mark, who came by now and then, he saw no one.
ch23.b003: On Friday the Master had died. Thomas accepted that as a fact. He had always been a man who accepted facts. What he could not accept was what came after. Late on Saturday night he had looked in for a few minutes at the upper chamber in the Mark home. He had looked around at the faces of his companions, faces broken by fear and grief and shame, and over those faces the events of the last three days had come crowding in all at once. He could not breathe. So he had turned without a word and walked out. He wanted to grieve alone. When he lost his twin sister at the age of nine, he had wept alone in just that way.
ch23.b004: On Sunday morning John Mark found him. Strange rumors were going around, he said. The tomb was empty; the women had seen something. Thomas listened. And he did not believe. People in grief see all sorts of things; that was the way of men, as he understood it. And yet that day he truly wanted to go back. If anyone had come for him, if Nathaniel or any two of the others had come and asked him to return, he would have gone. But having walked out the way he had the night before, he was too proud to go back so soon on his own feet. By the next day the gloom had sunk so deep that it took him nearly a week just to make up his mind.
ch23.b005: All that while the apostles waited for him. They stayed in Jerusalem, refusing to leave for Galilee without Thomas. And Thomas waited for them to come and seek him out. It was a week of each side waiting for the other.
ch23.b006: Sitting on the hillside, he went back over the last four years in reverse. The day he first met the Master at the landing at Tarichea, the Master had looked at him and told him he lacked faith, and then, in the same breath, that he received him: follow me. Thomas had never once forgotten those words. At first they had sounded like an insult; later, like a diagnosis; and at some point he could not name, like a promise. The promise that a man short of faith might still be received.
ch23.b007: He remembered, too, the day he knelt on the highland. The hands on his head. He still remembered their weight and their warmth. That day he had known they were not hands that took, though he could not have proved it. And now those hands had been pierced with nails. That he could prove. He had heard what was done to them. The things that could be proved, it seemed to him, were always the bad ones.
ch23.b008: He remembered the day they set out for Bethany. When the Master had said he would go into Judea on account of Lazarus, none of them had been able to stop him, and some had been reluctant even to go along. Thomas had been afraid too. He had been sure that they would kill him. And yet it was he who had brought his companions to their feet. If this was the Master’s choice, let them act like men of courage, he had said; let them go too, and die with him. He had said that. And when the Master did die, Thomas had not been there. None of them had died with him. Thomas tore up a handful of grass and let the wind take it.
ch23.b009: The Two Who Came for Him
ch23.b010: It was Saturday, after dark had fallen. Someone knocked at the door of Simon’s house. Thomas went out and found Peter and John standing there.
ch23.b011: Peter was out of breath. John stood quietly behind him, holding a lamp. For a while nobody spoke. Then Peter opened his mouth.
ch23.b013: That was all. Thomas did not know how to answer. The wish to blame them for being late and the wish to thank them for coming at all tangled together in his throat. In the end he picked up his cloak and went with them. That was his answer. When the time came to move, he had always been the first to move. It was about nine o’clock when the two of them found him, and before long the three were climbing the stairs of the Mark home.
ch23.b014: The next day his companions poured out their stories to him. Peter said he had met the Master in the garden. Ten of them said they had seen the Master inside the barred room. John said he had known from the start. The twins said their mother had talked with the Master. Thomas listened to it all. And he flatly refused to believe.
ch23.b015: “Peter has worked you all up,” he said. “This is the man who once saw the Master walking on the water.”
ch23.b016: Nathaniel reasoned with him. It did no good. Thomas’s doubt was no longer only doubt. There was stubbornness mixed into it now, and the shame of having run away from them. And there was one thing more mixed in, which Thomas himself did not notice. He did not mind the attention. The faces he had missed all week were all turned toward him now, every one of them trying to win him over. He sat in the seat of disagreement and warmed himself at their concern.
ch23.b017: Late that night, after the others had gone to their beds, Philip came and sat beside him. For a long while Philip said nothing. Then, abruptly, he spoke.
ch23.b018: “That was what I wanted most to know too. If he really has risen, whether his body still carries the marks of the cross.”
ch23.b019: Thomas turned his head and looked at Philip. Here was the man who always wanted to be shown, who would break in with some odd question even in the middle of the Master’s deepest teaching. Thomas had once thought him a little ridiculous. Even in doubting, he had told himself, his own doubt was analysis, while Philip’s was mere curiosity. Yet now Philip was sitting in exactly the same place he was. Philip said nothing more, got up, and went to his bed. It had not been a word of comfort, nor a word of persuasion. It had only been a way of saying: you are not alone.
ch23.b020: Thomas lay in the dark and thought of his house in Tarichea. His wife and four children. When he left home to become an apostle, his wife had been less sorry than relieved, relieved at the thought that her gloomy husband would be away most of the time. Thomas knew it and did not blame her. He was not an easy man to live with. Quarrelsome, suspicious first and last, a man who could go silent for days when the dark moods came. And these ten men had waited a whole week for such a man. They had not gone to Galilee; they had waited for him to come back. Thomas thought about that for a long time. And he was not yet willing to admit what it meant.
ch23.b022: On Sunday evening, a little after six o’clock, they sat down around the table. The doors were securely shut and barred. Peter sat on one side of Thomas and Nathaniel on the other. The lamplight trembled over the bread and the water jar.
ch23.b023: The talk turned again to the resurrection. Thomas put down his piece of bread and said that unless he saw the Master with his own eyes, and put his finger into the marks of the nails, he would not believe.
ch23.b024: The room went quiet. It was the most honest thing Thomas knew how to say. And the loneliest. He had asked to be shown. He had lived that way all his life: looking for the crack in the stone, checking the level, believing only what his hands could touch. That way had protected him. That way had left him alone.
ch23.b026: Inside the curve of the table, in the empty place where no one sat, a form was standing. The doors were still shut. The bars were still in place. The lamp flame did not so much as waver. He stood directly in front of Thomas.
ch23.b027: The Master first wished them all peace. And he told them he had waited a full week so that he might come again when every one of them was there together, and they could all hear once more his charge to carry the gospel of the kingdom into the whole world. Every one of them. Thomas heard it. A week. The very week he had spent wandering the hills. The Master had waited for him. While his companions were waiting for him, the Master had been waiting too.
ch23.b028: The Master told them that as the Father had sent him into the world, so he was sending them. They were to reveal the divine love not only with words but in their daily lives. They were not sent merely to love men’s souls; they were sent to love men. When the Spirit of Truth had come upon them, he said, they would not keep their light hidden behind closed doors like these. And what he asked of his disciples, he told them, was life itself: a life of loving service for their brothers in the flesh.
ch23.b029: Then the Master looked down into Thomas’s face.
ch23.b030: Thomas could not look away. Whenever he was at his lowest, he had always avoided meeting the Master. All this week he had been avoiding him. But now there was nowhere left to go.
ch23.b031: The Master spoke his name. Thomas. You said you would not believe unless you saw me and put your finger into the marks the nails left in my hands. Now you have seen me, and you have heard my words.
ch23.b032: And the Master held out his hands.
ch23.b033: Thomas looked at them. They were the hands that had rested on his head on the highland. He searched them for evidence, the way he had searched everything all his life. And there was nothing there. There were no nail marks. There was no wound. The very proof he had demanded, the very place he had sworn to put his finger, was empty.
ch23.b034: The Master told him that he would see no nail marks on these hands, because he had been raised in the form that Thomas himself would have when he left this world. So what would he say to his brothers now? And he went on: Thomas would acknowledge the truth, because even while he had been insisting so stoutly that he did not believe, in his heart he had already begun to believe.
ch23.b036: Already begun to believe. He heard it, and he knew it was true. When he tore up the grass on the hillside, when he mocked Peter, when he said those honest and lonely words at the table, something deep in him had already turned around. Only he had failed to see it. The Master had seen it all along.
ch23.b037: The Master called him by name and went on. Thomas’s doubts, he said, always dug in hardest at the very moment they were about to give way. He was not to be faithless but believing. And the Master said that he knew Thomas would believe, with his whole heart.
ch23.b038: Someone knew him like this. Knew the faith hiding behind the doubt, the longing hiding behind the stubbornness, even the small heart that had sat in the seat of disagreement warming itself. All his life Thomas had tried to explain himself, and he had never once succeeded. Yet now someone was reading him more truly than he had ever read himself. And having read him through, that someone did not reproach him.
ch23.b039: Thomas slid down from his place and fell to his knees. As he had on the highland. But this time no one had told him to kneel.
ch23.b041: His voice cracked. He said it again.
ch23.b043: These were not the words of a man who had surrendered to proof. They burst out of him in the place where there was no proof. The wound he had sworn to touch was never there. But he no longer needed it. Something greater than evidence was standing before him.
ch23.b044: Peter was weeping. Nathaniel laid his hand on Thomas’s back. One of the twins let out a small cry of wonder. These were the men who had sat beside him whenever the darkness came over him.
ch23.b045: The Master told Thomas that he had believed because he had truly seen and heard him. And he said that in the ages to come, those who believed without seeing with the eye of flesh or hearing with the mortal ear would be blessed.
ch23.b046: Thomas heard it on his knees. Those who believe without seeing. He could never be one of them. He had been a man who had to see. But now he could go to them. He could go to those who had not seen and tell them what he had seen. A doubter hears no voice so well as the voice of someone who has doubted too.
ch23.b047: Then the Master moved toward the head of the table, and he told them all to go to Galilee, where he would soon appear to them. And he vanished from their sight.
ch23.b048: No one slept easily that night either. They gathered in little groups by the lamps and talked in low voices. Thomas sat alone by the window. Nathaniel came over and sat down next to him. He looked down at Thomas’s hand and said, with a perfectly straight face:
ch23.b049: “About that finger of yours. What will you do with it, now that it’s out of work?”
ch23.b050: Thomas stared at him. And then he burst out laughing. It was the first laugh to break out of him in weeks. Somewhere in the middle of it, he realized that he was crying. Nathaniel said nothing and patted his shoulder. Perhaps, Thomas thought, the Master had put this man among the twelve for a day such as this.
ch23.b051: They called him Didymus, the Twin. Ever since he lost his twin sister at nine, he had lived as half of something. The world can take the dearest thing away at any moment: that was the lesson the little girl had left behind, and all his doubting had grown up out of it. But today he had seen what was taken come back. One whom even the tomb could not hold had passed through a closed door to find him. For the first time, Thomas felt that he might set down something he had been holding on to for a very long time.
ch23.b053: Very early the next morning, before the break of day, the eleven left Jerusalem and set out for Galilee. Every one of them was now fully convinced that the Master had risen from the dead. The man out in front, choosing the road, was Thomas.
ch23.b055: He said it. It was what he always said. It was the word of a man who argued against every dangerous road and then, once the decision was made, was the first on his feet. The others heard it and looked at one another and smiled. Thomas was back.
ch23.b056: Walking through the dark, Thomas looked down at his hand. He had said he would put this finger into the wound. In the end the finger had touched nothing at all. And yet he was walking now, for the first time in his life, without doubt. No; the doubt was not gone. He knew himself. Doubt would come for him again. But now he knew that it shouted loudest at the very moment it was about to crumble. And he knew that beyond the shouting, someone was waiting for him.
ch23.b057: The words he had first heard at the landing in Tarichea came back to him. You lack faith; nevertheless, I receive you. Four years on, those words had at last been made whole. The man who lacked faith had become a man who would go to the countless many who would believe without seeing.
ch23.b058: The eastern sky was growing faintly light. Thomas quickened his pace. Galilee was waiting.
ch23.b060: The course of events follows 191:5, “Appearance to Thomas.” Thomas’s leaving the upper chamber late on Saturday night for the home of Simon in Bethpage (189:4.1); John Mark’s finding him, the pride and depression that kept him away for a week, the apostles’ refusal to go to Galilee without him, and Peter and John bringing him back on Saturday evening (191:0.12–0.13, 191:5.1); his refusal the next day to believe his companions, his claim that Peter had stirred them up, Nathaniel’s reasoning with him, and his unconscious enjoyment of their attention (191:5.1); and the words at supper, the appearance of the Master, the absence of nail marks, Thomas’s confession, the saying about those who believe without seeing, the instruction to go to Galilee, and the departure before dawn the next morning (191:5.2–5.7) all rest on the text.
ch23.b061: The words at Tarichea (138:5.1), the loss of his twin sister, his “Let’s go,” and his avoiding Jesus when depressed (139:8.8–8.11), his words on the way to Bethany (167:4.7), his wife’s relief at his leaving home (139:8.3), and Philip’s question about the marks of the crucifixion (191:0.9) are taken from Papers 138, 139, 167, and 191.
ch23.b062: Added fiction includes Thomas’s inner thoughts and the shape of his memories, the hillside scenery, Peter’s brief words at the door, Philip’s visit in the night, Nathaniel’s joke about the finger and the scene by the window, Thomas’s jibe about Peter seeing the Master on the water, the Master’s gesture of holding out his hands (the text says only that no nail marks were to be seen), the companions’ gestures after the confession, and Thomas saying “Let’s go” at the departure. Thomas’s confession is rendered with a slight variation from the cry recorded in the text.
ch23.b063: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
ch24.title: Morning by the Sea of Galilee
ch24.b002: The eleven left Jerusalem very early on Monday morning, before the eastern sky had begun to pale. Thomas walked at the head and chose the road. Matthew Levi kept to the rear of the little company, and at his belt hung a leather purse. A week earlier David Zebedee had dropped it into his lap without a word and gone away again; it held every coin the apostles had left. Matthew still found it awkward to wear. With each stride the purse knocked against his thigh, and he could not stop thinking that another man had walked exactly like this for three years, with the same weight swinging at his side.
ch24.b003: They were well past Bethany when they heard someone running up behind them. It was John Mark. The boy had slipped out of the city on their heels and trailed them at a distance, and only when he judged that they had come too far to send him home did he walk boldly up into their midst. Peter laughed aloud. Nobody sent him back. Matthew looked at the young face beside him and thought of the house it belonged to. In his father’s upper chamber they had eaten the last supper, had hidden behind barred doors, had twice seen the Master alive. This boy had kept watch with them through every one of those days.
ch24.b004: They did not hurry. Whenever the road brought them to a village they stopped, and they told the people that the Master had risen from the dead and that they had seen him with their own eyes. At first their voices shook. A week before, they had been men who sat in a locked room and started at every footstep on the stair. But the more often they told it, the steadier their voices grew. Matthew watched the change come over his brethren, and he heard it come over himself as well. The voice that had once counted coins at a customs table was standing before strangers and bearing witness to a man who had come back from the grave.
ch24.b005: Because they paused so often to tell the story, it was very late on Wednesday night when they reached Bethsaida. Zebedee’s house took them in, and they slept where they fell. It was noon on Thursday before they were all awake and ready to sit down to breakfast. One place was empty. Simon Zelotes had grown quieter and darker the nearer they came to Galilee, and when they reached Bethsaida he left his brethren and went home to Capernaum. No one had been able to hold him.
ch24.b006: Matthew had watched Simon the whole way north. Simon walked in the middle of the company but spoke to no one. Once, as they climbed the Jordan valley, he stopped and stood a long while looking at the northern sky. Beyond it lay Galilee, and beyond Galilee the old comrades he had left behind when he followed the Master. Matthew could guess what sat on that man’s back. To a Zealot a tax collector was a dog of Rome, and four years ago Simon had hardly been able to bear sitting at the same table with him. Since then the two had drawn slowly closer. On the night of the ordination, when Matthew stumbled on a threshold in the dark, it was Simon’s hand that caught him. Yet now Matthew could find nothing to say. Here were a publican who had never learned how to comfort and a Zealot who did not know how to be comforted. So Matthew did the one thing he could think of: at every halt along the road he sat down next to Simon. And Simon did not send him away.
ch24.b008: They spent Thursday afternoon and the early evening waiting at Zebedee’s house. The Master had told them he would meet them in Galilee, but he had not said when, or where. As the sun went down, Peter stood up and said he was going fishing. Every one of them said he would go too. They were worn out with waiting, and they missed the feel of work they knew. When Peter took hold of the net, his hands remembered before his mind did. For four years he had all but let that work go, yet his hands had not forgotten it.
ch24.b009: All night they cast the nets, and all night they caught nothing. Nobody much minded. There in the boat they talked through the dark hours about everything that had happened to them in Jerusalem: the empty tomb, the garden, the shut room, Thomas on his knees. There was so much to tell. The nets came up empty, but their hearts did not. John leaned against the gunwale and watched the stars go out one by one. Four years ago, on this same water, he had sat mending nets with his father. In those days the lake had been the whole of his world.
ch24.b010: When the east began to brighten, they decided to put back to Bethsaida. As they drew near the usual landing place, they could see someone on the beach, standing beside a fire. At first they took him for John Mark, come down to meet them and help bring in the catch. But the closer they came, the plainer it was that they had been wrong. The man was too tall to be John Mark. It did not cross anyone’s mind that it might be the Master.
ch24.b012: It was about six o’clock on Friday morning, April 21. As they let down the anchor and made ready to climb into the small boat and go ashore, the man on the beach called out to them, asking the lads whether they had caught anything. They called back that they had not. It was the kind of question every fisherman on that lake heard often; at sunrise the fish merchants of Tarichea were usually on the shore, ready to buy fresh catches for the drying sheds, and they hailed the boats in just that way. Then the man spoke again. He told them to throw the net on the right side of the boat and they would find fish. They had no idea who he was. Yet with one mind they did as he said.
ch24.b013: At once the net grew heavy, so full that they could barely drag it up. John felt the weight of it through his hands, and in that moment he knew. He had always been the first to see. He leaned across and whispered in Peter’s ear.
ch24.b015: Peter did not stop to think. He had never been a man who thought first and moved afterward. He sprang up and threw himself into the sea to reach the Master a little sooner. The cold water rose to his chest, and he waded and thrashed his way toward the shore. His brethren followed close behind in the small boat, towing the net full of fish after them. John, pulling at the oar, watched Peter in the water ahead. On the morning they ran to the tomb, John had been the faster. Today Peter was in front. John thought that was right. This ought to be Peter’s day.
ch24.b016: By now John Mark was up and out of the house. Seeing the apostles coming ashore with the laden net, he ran down the beach to meet them, and then he saw that there were eleven men, not ten. He guessed who the stranger must be. The boy ran straight to him and knelt at his feet, calling him his Lord and his Master. The other ten stood by in astonished silence.
ch24.b017: The Master spoke to the boy, and it was not with the greeting of peace he had used in Jerusalem. He spoke in the most ordinary tone in the world. He told John Mark he was glad to see him again, and glad to be in carefree Galilee where they could have a good visit together, and he asked him to stay and eat breakfast with them. The apostles heard that voice. It was the voice they had listened to for four years, on this shore and on these hills and in these fishing boats. They were so dumbfounded that they forgot to haul the net up onto the beach. Then the Master told them to bring in some of their catch and cook it for breakfast; the fire was already lit, he said, and there was bread enough.
ch24.b019: Peter came up out of the water and stood on the beach. And then he saw it: a fire of charcoal glowing among the stones at the water’s edge. A thin smoke rose from the red coals. He caught the smell of it, and he knew that smell.
ch24.b020: His breath stopped. The courtyard of Annas. The chilly night. The charcoal fire where he had stood among the servants warming his hands. The face of the serving girl in its light. Are you not one of this man’s disciples? I am not. Beside that fire he had denied his Master, and not only once; again and again the words had come out of him until the cock crowed. And three years and more before that, beside another fire in Zebedee’s garden, he had sworn that whatever came, none of them would ever turn back. The two fires swam together before his eyes, the fire of the vow and the fire of the denial. And now a third fire was burning at his feet. The Master had kindled this one.
ch24.b021: Peter swayed, but he did not fall. The words he had heard in the garden held him up: that he had been forgiven even before he asked. He gathered himself together and went down on his knees at the Master’s feet, the sea water dripping from his clothes.
ch24.b023: It was all he could say. It was enough. In the courtyard of Annas the fire had warmed his body and frozen him within. This fire was different. Before this fire there was nothing he needed to hide. The one who knew everything had lit it, and had been waiting beside it for him.
ch24.b024: Peter rose and went to help the others haul in the net. When they had dragged the catch up the beach and counted it, there were one hundred and fifty-three large fish. A murmur of wonder went round among them. Yet there was no miracle in it. The Master had known the fish were there, and so he had told them where to cast; that was all. Standing beside the men who were counting, Matthew counted along with them in his head. It was an old habit. One hundred and fifty-three. He would remember that number for a long time.
ch24.b025: The Master told them all to come and eat. And he said that even the twins should sit down while he talked with them; John Mark would clean the fish. The twins looked at each other. They were always the ones who fed everyone else: before five thousand on the hillside, before the twelve, before the ten in the upper chamber. And now the Master was telling them to sit. For a moment they did not know what to do with themselves. Then they sat down side by side on the sand, and the same smile spread over both their faces.
ch24.b026: John Mark brought seven fish of good size, and the Master laid them on the fire. When they were cooked, the boy carried them round to the ten. The Master broke the bread and handed it to John Mark, and the boy passed it to the hungry apostles. When everyone had been served, the Master told the lad to sit down, and with his own hands he served him fish and bread. Matthew watched. It was always so with the Master. He served the one who served, and he served him last.
ch24.b027: While they ate, the Master talked with them. He talked about the things they had lived through together in Galilee, by this very lake: the day they first left their nets to follow him, the weeks of going two by two from village to village, the evening the crowds came and the bread ran short, the night of the storm. For more than an hour they sat round the fire and listened. It was as though nothing had happened in Jerusalem at all. Or rather, it was as though, because Jerusalem had happened, these memories were becoming theirs all over again. The sun climbed high above the water. The surface of the lake glittered. Gulls cried overhead. Matthew thought of the Master’s words: carefree Galilee. It was true. This morning, at least, it was true.
ch24.b029: When breakfast was finished, the Master beckoned to Peter and to John to come and walk with him along the shore. The three set off across the wet sand, and the others stayed by the fire.
ch24.b030: As they walked, the Master turned first to John and asked him whether he loved him. John did not hesitate. With his whole heart, he answered. Then, the Master said, he must give up his intolerance and learn to love men the way he himself had been loved. He was to spend his life proving that nothing in the world is greater than love. It is God’s love, the Master told him, that moves men to seek salvation, and love is the root from which all spiritual goodness grows, the very heart of what is true and beautiful.
ch24.b031: Intolerance. John felt his face grow hot at the word. He remembered: the strangers teaching in the Master’s name whom he had ordered to stop; the Samaritan village that would not receive them, and how he had wanted to call fire down from heaven upon it; the days when he had been quietly proud to be one of the three who stood closest to the Master. He had believed that pride had burned away at Golgotha. But the Master knew its root was still there. John bowed his head. And he understood that this was not a rebuke but a charge. It was a whole life’s work being put into his hands.
ch24.b032: Then the Master turned to Peter and asked whether he loved him. Peter answered that the Lord knew he loved him with all his soul. If so, the Master said, then he must feed his lambs. He must never neglect to care for the weak, the poor, and the young. He must preach the gospel without fear and without favoring anyone, and always remember that God does not judge men by their station. He must serve others as he had been served, and forgive others as he had been forgiven. And he must let the things he lived through teach him the worth of meditation and of thoughtful reflection.
ch24.b033: They walked on a little farther, and the Master asked again whether Peter really loved him. Yes, Lord, Peter said; the Lord knew that he did. Then let him take good care of the Master’s sheep, Jesus said. He was to be a good and true shepherd to the flock and never betray their trust in him. He must not let the enemy catch him unawares. He must keep on guard always, watching and praying.
ch24.b034: Watch. The word went into Peter like a thorn. In Gethsemane the Master had told him to watch and pray. He had slept. And when he woke, he had drawn his sword. A man who slept when he should have watched and struck when he should have been still: the Master knew all of that, and still he was handing him the flock.
ch24.b035: A few steps more, and the Master turned to him a third time and asked whether he truly loved him.
ch24.b036: Peter stopped walking. A third time. Three questions, and how many denials beside the fire in the courtyard? More than three. He had stopped counting that night. And here, on a beach where the charcoal still sent up its thread of smoke, the Master had asked him three times. Did the Master not trust him? The hurt rose into his throat, and he spoke with more feeling than he could master.
ch24.b037: “Lord, you know everything. You know that I truly love you.”
ch24.b038: His voice cracked. The Master looked at him. It was the same look that had found him on the porch of Annas. And he told Peter to feed his sheep. He must not forsake the flock. He must be an example and a strength to all his fellow shepherds. He must love the flock as he himself had been loved, and give himself for their good just as the Master had given his own life for Peter’s good. And he must follow after him even to the end.
ch24.b039: To the end. Peter heard it, and at last he understood. The three questions were not a sign of doubt. Wherever he had broken down, the Master was setting a stone back in place. The mouth that had disowned him was being given the chance to confess its love, and with each confession came a task: the lambs, the sheep, the flock. The hurt melted, and tears came in its place. Peter did not weep aloud. The wind off the sea dried his wet face.
ch24.b040: Yet Peter was still Peter. He took that last word, to follow on to the end, quite literally. He turned and pointed at John, who was walking a little behind them, and asked what this man would do if Peter followed after the Master. The Master saw that he had misunderstood and told him not to trouble himself over what his brethren would do. If it were the Master’s will that John should stay on after Peter was gone, even until he came again, what was that to Peter? Peter need only make sure that he himself followed.
ch24.b041: John, listening, had to keep from laughing. It was such a Peter question. A moment ago the man had been weeping, and already he was worrying about someone else’s future. Afterward the remark spread among the brethren, and it was taken to mean that John would not die before the Master came back to set up his kingdom in power and glory. Many wanted to believe it. And in time that belief would do a great deal to bring one man back to his feet. That man was Simon Zelotes.
ch24.b043: When the three came back to the fire, the Master took Andrew and James and walked with them. He asked Andrew whether he trusted him. The man who had once been chief of the apostles stopped where he stood and answered that he trusted him, most certainly, and that the Master knew it. Then, the Master said, if Andrew trusted him, he must trust his brethren more, even Peter. Once the Master had trusted Andrew with the leadership of the others; now, as he was going to the Father, Andrew must trust others in turn. When persecution came and the brethren began to scatter, they would lay heavy burdens on James, the Master’s brother in the flesh, burdens he had no experience to carry, and Andrew must be a wise and thoughtful counselor to him. And Andrew must go on trusting, for the Master would not fail him.
ch24.b044: Even Peter. Andrew stood still a long time with those words. The Master knew about that evening in the upper chamber, when Andrew had risen and undercut his brother’s report. He had not scolded him for it. He had only shown him the way. An eye that reads men well is not enough, he seemed to say; to that eye you must add a heart that trusts. Andrew nodded. He looked across at his brother sitting by the fire, and he saw that Peter’s back was a little straighter than it used to be.
ch24.b045: The Master asked James Zebedee too whether he trusted him. James answered that he did, with all his heart. If he trusted the Master more, Jesus told him, he would be less impatient with his brethren. He must learn to weigh what his words and his deeds would bring about, and remember that a man reaps what he sows. He was to pray for a quiet spirit and grow in patience, for these would hold him up when the hour came to drink the cup of sacrifice. James listened without a word. He did not yet know what that cup would be.
ch24.b046: Thomas and Nathaniel came next. The Master asked Thomas whether he served him, and Thomas said that he did, now and always. The Master told him he must stop doubting. He must believe in God like a child but stop behaving like one. He must take courage and grow strong in faith. To Nathaniel he said that he should mix friendship into his counsel and add love to his philosophy. He should be less critical, and expect less of some men, and so spare himself some disappointment. On the way back Nathaniel murmured to Thomas that the two of them had been read rather accurately. Thomas tried not to smile, and failed.
ch24.b048: Next the Master walked with Matthew and Philip. He asked Philip whether he obeyed him, and Philip said he would obey him even with his life. Then the Master told him to go into the lands of the gentiles and proclaim the gospel. He must stop being afraid of men. And from now on, the Master said, Philip would no longer be kept busy with money and supplies; he was free, just like his brethren, to preach the good news. Philip looked down at his empty hands. For four years those hands had always carried a sack and always kept a tally. Now they were empty, and they felt strangely light.
ch24.b049: Then the Master looked at Matthew and asked whether it was in his heart to obey him. Matthew answered: Yes, Lord. He had given himself entirely to doing the Master’s will.
ch24.b050: If he would obey, the Master said, he must now go out and teach the good news of the kingdom to all peoples. No longer would he supply his brethren with the material things of life. From now on he too must proclaim the good news of salvation of the spirit.
ch24.b051: Matthew’s step faltered. No longer would he supply his brethren with the material things of life. He heard the words again inside himself. That had been his work: raising the money. As the fiscal agent of the apostolic corps he had carried that charge for years. Of course that was what the Master meant. Of course it was. And yet, deep in Matthew’s chest, one small question lifted its head. Could it be? All the gaps he had quietly filled when no one was looking, all the money he had given in the names of other believers, the secret he had so often burned to tell whenever someone looked down on him for what he had been. Could it be that the Master…?
ch24.b052: He looked at the Master’s face. The Master was looking at him. There was nothing in those eyes that answered him. They might have been the eyes of someone who knew everything, or simply the eyes of a friend. Matthew did not ask. He could not ask. It was only his own longing talking, he told himself, an old publican’s old wish clutching at a single phrase on a bright morning. But even after he had pushed the thought away, his shoulders felt lighter. He heard the Master go on: Matthew must remember that Jew and gentile alike were his brothers; he must fear no one; and where the Master was going, Matthew would soon come.
ch24.b053: Where I am going. Matthew took the words and held them. All his life he had been trying to prove something: that a tax collector could be clean, that a tax collector’s money could serve a holy work. And this man had never once asked him to prove anything. He had only told him to follow, just as he had at the customs table. Matthew touched the purse at his belt. He knew the day would come when he set it down. When that day came, he thought, he would not be sorry.
ch24.b054: Last of all the Master walked with the Alpheus twins, James and Judas. He asked whether they believed in him, and both of them answered together that they did. He told them they were his apostles and always would be. After he was gone, even if they should go back to the work they used to do, they must go on believing and remember the days they had spent with him. They must never let a change in their outward work shake their loyalty. Nothing a son of God does is common, he told them, so from now on they should do their work as if for God. The twins understood every word. For the first time, they understood something the Master had said from beginning to end.
ch24.b055: It was almost ten o’clock when he came back from his walk with the twins. Before he left them, he asked that two of the apostles volunteer to go to Simon Zelotes and bring him back that very day. Peter and Andrew stood up, the two brothers together. Then the Master told them all that he would meet them at noon the next day on the mount of their ordination, and he vanished from their sight.
ch24.b057: That afternoon Peter and Andrew went to Capernaum. Simon Zelotes was sitting in the courtyard of his house. He saw them come in and did not get up. Peter told him what had happened on the beach that morning: the charcoal fire, the hundred and fifty-three fish, the walks two by two along the shore. And he said the Master had asked for Simon to be brought back. Simon was silent a long time. At last he spoke.
ch24.b059: “He did. He said it had to be today.”
ch24.b060: It was Andrew who answered. He added nothing to what his brother had said. With those few words he simply stood surety that his brother’s story was true. Simon got up and took his cloak. That evening the eleven were together again in Zebedee’s house. When Simon came through the door, the first to rise was Matthew. Without a word he broke off a piece of bread and held it out to Simon. Simon took it. It was bread from a publican’s hand. He looked down at it a long while, and then he ate. Neither man said anything. Andrew saw it all, and for once he wanted to say something: that it had been well done. But this time too, the words never quite reached his lips.
ch24.b061: The next day, Saturday, April 22, at noon, the eleven climbed the hill near Capernaum. It was the very height where, three years and more before, the Master had set them apart as his apostles. The winter grass of that day had given way to the new grass of spring. To the south the Sea of Galilee shone in the sunlight. And the Master appeared among them.
ch24.b062: They knelt in a circle around him, as they had that day. He repeated the charges he had given them when he first set them apart, and he enacted the ordination over again before their eyes. John, kneeling, looked round the circle. Eleven men. The place where the first hand had rested on that winter afternoon was empty. No one moved to fill it. The circle stood a little open on that side and left the place as it was. John looked at the gap and thought of Judas, of the hand that had sat plucking at blades of grass that day. He prayed for that hand. It was all he could do.
ch24.b063: But the Master’s prayer was not the prayer of that first day. It was the voice of one who held all power and authority in his own universe, speaking with the rulers of the universes. The apostles had never heard words of such majesty. He stayed with them on the mount just one hour. Then he took a tender farewell of them and vanished from their sight. For the rest of their lives the eleven never forgot that hour, in which they gave themselves once more to their pledge as his ambassadors.
ch24.b064: After that, for a full week, no one saw the Master. They stayed on at Bethsaida. They did not even dare go out fishing, for fear that he might come while they were away and they would miss him. On Saturday, April 29, at three in the afternoon, more than five hundred believers from around Capernaum gathered at Bethsaida by the shore. Peter preached to them, his first public sermon since the resurrection, and he was at his best. As he brought his sermon to a close, he declared that Jesus of Nazareth was not dead, that he had risen from the tomb, and that they themselves had seen him and spoken with him. The words were barely out of his mouth when the Master appeared at his side, in full view of everyone. He wished them peace and was gone. John, standing among his brethren, watched Peter. His voice did not tremble. That voice, which had trembled so beside the charcoal fire.
ch24.b066: Early the next morning they set out for Jerusalem. They taught and preached all the way down the Jordan, and so it was late on Wednesday, May 3, before they reached the home of the Marks. Grief was waiting for them there. Only a few hours earlier, John Mark’s father, Elijah Mark, had died without warning. The apostles were sure of the resurrection of the dead, and the thought comforted them, yet it did not take away all their sorrow. This was the man who had sheltered them in their darkest days. The boy comforted his mother, and speaking for her, he asked the apostles to go on making her house their home. The upper chamber became theirs once again.
ch24.b067: Early on Thursday morning, May 18, as the eleven were sitting down to breakfast in that upper chamber, the Master appeared to them. He told them to stay in Jerusalem until he sent them the Spirit of Truth, who would soon be poured out upon all flesh and would clothe them with power from on high. Then Simon Zelotes broke in. Was the Master now going to restore the kingdom? Would they see the glory of God shown on earth?
ch24.b068: No one in the room was surprised. Simon was Simon. The Master looked at him and told him that he was still holding on to his old ideas of the Jewish Messiah and an earthly kingdom. But when the spirit came upon them, the Master said, they would receive spiritual power and go out into all the world preaching this gospel. There was no reproach in his voice. There was patience, as there always had been with Simon, all four years. Simon bowed his head. He did not yet understand it all. But he knew that the Master had borne with him to the very end.
ch24.b069: The Master went on. As the Father had sent him into the world, he told them, so he was sending them. They must love one another and trust one another. Then he spoke the name of Judas. Judas was no longer with them, he said, because his love had grown cold and because he had refused to trust his loyal brethren. Had they not read in the Scriptures that it is not good for man to be alone? Had he not sent them out two and two, so that they would not grow lonely and fall into the harm that isolation brings? Even in the flesh, he reminded them, he had never let himself be alone for long; even when he communed with the Father he had always kept two or three of them near him. So they must trust each other and confide in each other. That was all the more needful now, because today he was leaving them alone in the world.
ch24.b070: Matthew closed his eyes as he listened. Confide in one another. He was a man carrying a secret he had never told. And yet he was not Judas. He had gone to the Master; he had stayed beside his brethren; he had learned to sit at the same fire as Simon Zelotes. Judas had done none of these things. Matthew thought about how small that difference was, and how great. Andrew was thinking along the same lines. He was thinking of a certain dawn, and a man sitting alone under a fig tree.
ch24.b071: When the Master had finished speaking, he beckoned them to come with him. He led them out of the upper chamber and on toward the Mount of Olives. No one spoke a single word, not through the streets, not across the Kidron valley, not up the long slope. At about half past seven they came to the western slope of Olivet, some two thirds of the way up the mountain. From there the whole city lay open to view. And below them lay Gethsemane, the olive trees of the night he was arrested.
ch24.b072: The Master stood before them. No one told them to, but the eleven knelt around him in a circle, as they had on the mount of ordination. It was the third time. It would be the last.
ch24.b073: He told them to remain in Jerusalem until they were clothed with power from on high. He was going up now to the Father, he said, and very soon the Spirit of Truth would be sent into this world. When the spirit came, they were to begin the proclamation of the kingdom afresh, in Jerusalem first and then to the farthest ends of the earth. They were to love men as he had loved them, and serve men as he had served them. They were to remember everything he had taught them and the life he had lived among them. His love would cover them, his spirit would dwell with them, and his peace would rest upon them. And he bade them farewell.
ch24.b074: Then he vanished from their sight. It was about a quarter to eight. It was no different from all the other times he had disappeared. There was no cloud, no burst of light, no thunder. The morning sun simply went on shining on the place where he had stood.
ch24.b075: For a long while the eleven stayed on their knees without moving. Simon Zelotes was staring at the spot where the Master had been. The kingdom had not been restored. The glory of God had not come down like lightning upon the earth. And yet he did not fall apart as he had after the upper chamber. Right to the end, the Master had taken his foolish question and borne with it, as he had for four years. Simon did not yet fully understand what that patience was. But he resolved to follow it and find out. It was unlike any banner he had ever followed. Peter was the first to lift his head. He looked down at Gethsemane below. There he had slept, and drawn his sword, and run. And now here he was. Follow me to the end: he heard it again. John was looking at Jerusalem. North of the wall he could make out the low hill of Golgotha. On that hill he had stood to the end. Now he would have to stand to the end somewhere else, in the place where love is proved the greatest thing in the world.
ch24.b076: Matthew got to his feet and brushed the dust from his knees. The purse at his belt swung. Later that morning, at the Marks’ house, before one hundred and twenty disciples, the apostles cast lots for the man who would take the place of Judas. The lot fell on Matthias, and he was made treasurer. The purse passed into new hands, the purse that for three years had hung at one man’s belt. From now on it would serve not the counting but the telling. Matthew looked down at his empty hands. Philip was standing beside him. The two of them looked at each other’s empty hands and smiled.
ch24.b078: The events follow Papers 192–193: the eleven leaving for Galilee with John Mark following them past Bethany, their preaching on the way and late arrival at Bethsaida on Wednesday night (192:0.4–5); Simon Zelotes going home in despondency (192:1.10); the fruitless night, the figure on the beach, the net cast on the right side, John’s recognition and Peter’s plunge, John Mark’s homage, Peter’s shock at the charcoal fire, the 153 fish, the twins told to sit, the breakfast, and the fish merchants of Tarichea (192:1.1–9); the talks two by two and Peter and Andrew fetching Simon Zelotes (192:1.10–2.14); the saying about John that helped bring Simon Zelotes back (192:2.6); the appearance on the mount of ordination, the week of waiting, Peter’s first public sermon and the appearance beside him (192:3.1–4.3); the return to Jerusalem and the death of Elijah Mark (192:4.4–5); the appearance in the upper chamber on May 18, Simon Zelotes’s question, the words about Judas, the silent walk to Olivet, the farewell and the hour of the ascension, and the choice of Matthias (193:3.1–3, 193:5.1–5, 193:6.1–3). Character facts come from Paper 139: Matthew’s secret giving, which Jesus knew of though Matthew hardly realized it (139:7.8–9); Simon Zelotes’s home in Capernaum, his nationalism, and Jesus’ patience with him (139:11.1, 11.4, 11.9); John as first to recognize the Master on the shore (139:4.10) and his intolerance (139:4.8); Peter’s denials in the courtyard of Annas (184:2.4–8).
ch24.b079: Added as fiction: the inner thoughts and memories of Peter, John, Matthew and Andrew; the scenery of the shore, the hill and Olivet; Matthew’s feelings about the purse and his half-formed hope that the Master’s words to him touched his secret (left deliberately uncertain); Nathaniel’s aside to Thomas; Matthew sitting beside Simon Zelotes on the road and handing him bread on his return (continuing the threshold scene of the ordination night, 140:6); Simon Zelotes’s thoughts after the ascension; the short exchange in Capernaum; the empty place of Judas in the circle on the mount; and the smile Matthew and Philip share over their empty hands. Peter’s cry and his third answer follow the sense of the text in different words. The link Peter feels between the three questions and his denials is shown only as his own thought; the text records that he denied the Master repeatedly, more than three times, and the chapter keeps to that.
ch24.b080: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
